# How to use this booklet {.unnumbered}

This is the exercise booklet for **Module 3** of the Health Data Science MSc.
It is organised by teaching day: each day is a part of the book, and each
chapter inside a day is one exercise you can finish in a single sitting.

**Everything here runs in your browser.** The code cells are live — editable,
runnable, with their output appearing underneath. There is nothing to install
before the first session and nothing to download. R and Python are both
compiled to WebAssembly and fetched by the page itself.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What to expect the first time you press Run
The first cell on a page takes roughly ten to thirty seconds, because the
browser is downloading R or Python and the packages the page needs — about 48 MB
for the R side, 15 MB for the Python side. After that it is cached, and every
cell is immediate. On a slow connection, open the page and run the first cell
before the session starts.
:::

Each page is a **separate session**. Objects you create in Exercise 1.1 do not
exist in Exercise 1.2, which is why @sec-shift rebuilds its model in the first
cell rather than loading one from Exercise 1.2. Within a page, cells share
everything, top to bottom.

## Why both languages

Most health data science teams use one language for data management and the
other for modelling, and the ability to read a colleague's code in the language
you do not prefer is worth more than fluency in either. Every exercise therefore
has an R path and a Python path doing the same work, in tabs. The booklet is
explicit about the places where the two genuinely differ rather than pretending
one is a translation of the other.

## What each chapter looks like

1. **Objectives** — what you will be able to do, phrased so you can test whether
   you can do it.
2. **Worked example** — cells that run themselves when the page loads. Nothing
   is hidden; the point is to see a correct pipeline before you build one.
3. **Tasks** — cells with `______` for you to fill in. Most have a *Hint*
   button, and a *Check yourself* call that inspects the object you just made.
4. **Stretch** — optional, for when you finish early. Not harder versions of the
   task; the question the task raises.
5. **What you can and cannot now claim** — the sentences you could defend to a
   clinician on the basis of what you just did, and the ones you could not.

## The self-checks

Tasks call helpers such as `check_split()` or `check_beats_baseline()`. They are
not graded and nothing is submitted. They exist because the most expensive
mistake in a first ML pipeline is not a wrong answer but a silently wrong
object — a split that leaks, a column read as text, a model fitted to the test
set — which produces a number that looks entirely reasonable. Each check prints
what it inspected, so a failure points you at where to look.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A check that passes does not mean your answer is right. It means your answer is
not wrong in the specific way the check knows about.
:::

## Working offline, or in RStudio

If you would rather work on your own machine — and you will want to for the
assignment — @sec-setup is the install guide. The code is identical; only the
`library()` lines differ slightly, because the browser loads individual
`tidymodels` packages rather than the metapackage, to keep the download small.

## Where the data comes from

Every dataset here is **simulated**, by a script you can read:
`scripts/make_data.R`. Because we wrote the data-generating process, we know the
true answer to every question asked, so you can find out whether your diagnosis
was *right* rather than merely *plausible* — a luxury you will never have again
once you work with real patient data. @sec-data gives the generating equations
and the known defects of each file.
